title: From terror to triumph on the track:
article: Deng Kuol Marial used to run from danger in his native Sudan. Now, he runs for athletic glory.

The interview with Deng Kuol Marial, St. Lawrence College's gifted cross-country racer, begins with a glance at his youth in and around his native Sudan, Africa's largest country. We say in and around because the kid certainly travelled, always out of sheer necessity, often as a minute piece of a migrating mass of refugees.
Quickly, one learns his was no run-of-the-mill childhood.
"One day soldiers came and I was given a gun," the soft-spoken second-year Police Foundations student recalled.
"They said they were training all young people to fight, but nobody fools you. If you don't accept, if you don't hold the gun, people will kill you."
"How old were you?" he's asked.
"Five."
Deng wisely shouldered the Russian-made AK-47 and lived to breathe another day, which in reality became the daily objective.
He was separated from his mother. A decade would pass before the two again laid eyes on one another.

The 1983 Sudan civil war claimed two million lives and displaced four million others. The extensive Kuol clan - the patriarch, Deng's dad, has eight wives and has fathered "more than 50 children" - contributed to both macabre categories.

During one unsettling journey toward a more hopeful existence, more than 150 children perished, some from starvation and disease, most at the hands of soldiers carrying out murderous middle-of-the- night attacks.
"You come to realize that people who are with you that morning will die later that same day," Deng said. "This happened many times. I lost step-brothers and friends."
As an eight-year-old, he and others were held captive in a stifling container for two weeks.
"What did they feed you?" he's asked.
"Feed?" he replied incredulously. "You don't eat anything. The only way we survived was to drink our \[urine\]."

This wretched, nomadic existence took him to Ethiopia, Eritrea, Uganda, Kenya and Egypt. They would stay a few months, even a year or two, existing primarily off provisions from United Nations relief agencies.
He even swam up the Nile River and into Egypt, Deng and 130 others.
The swim was his idea, he pointed out proudly. "Soldiers were chasing us for three months straight, never letting up. We were always moving, moving, moving.
"We didn't know where we were. Someone said, 'Deng! You are smart. Which way do we go?'
"I said we should swim with the current, which would take us to Egypt.
"It took us six days but we made it," he said. Twenty others who began the treacherous trip perished en route.

Besides the unrelenting soldiers, the swimmers had to avoid becoming a midday snack for the formidable Nile crocodile. They did this by boiling the leaves of the khanack tree, said Deng, then coating themselves in the pungent liquid.
"Crocodiles do not like the smell, they will swim away from you," he said. "There were people who did not spread it on themselves. Some were taken by the crocodile."

Deng was born in the southern Sudan village of Bor, near the ancient capital of Khartoum. He is a member of Sudan's most populous tribe, the Dinka. His father, Kuol, was a commander in the southern Sudan army. He has since retired.
His mother, Ayen, gave birth to a dozen children, Deng being the second youngest.
He immigrated to Canada four years ago with his brother Abraham, settling in London, where the rake-thin youngster with the cautious eyes starred on the Central Catholic High School soccer club.
A school track coach, impressed by the kid's speed and stamina on the soccer pitch, persuaded Deng to take up running.
Back home, Deng Kuol ran only to save his skin. "Running was something I did to escape and survive," he said. "Besides, I loved soccer too much, and I was good."
He showed natural ability on the track, if not a sound understanding of the relay race format.

In his debut meet, he anchored Central's entry in a four-man distance relay and crossed the finish line in second place. Unaware the race had ended, Deng continued on. "I ran three more laps," he said, chuckling.

Last year the Vikings' rookie captured a gold medal at the Ontario Colleges Athletic Association cross-country championship. His time of 26 minutes, five seconds in the eight-kilometre jaunt marked a personal best and beat the runner-up by 29 seconds.
Two weeks ago in Brockville, the shy, five-foot-eight runner eclipsed 26 minutes to claim a second straight OCAA gold, this time with an astonishing 89-
second victory margin.

"He possesses a huge amount of natural talent," said St. Lawrence cross-country coach Laura Fluit. "He works hard and he's very focused. His goal this year was to break 26 minutes for eight kilometres. He focused on it and he ran 25:52 in the \[OCAA\] final."
Mind you, focusing on a foot-race is child's play for someone who spent 10 years focusing desperately on how to survive until the next sunrise.
Despite the despair and hardship of his formative years in Africa, one memory warms Deng with instant joy each time it's rekindled.

Five years ago in Nairobi, where Deng attended high school, the 15-year-old headed out for a morning class. Standing outside the cramped flat he shared with several others was an elderly woman. Neither recognized the other at first, but soon they embraced.
Deng's mother, told of her son's whereabouts, had set out on foot - barefoot - and walked for two months to reunite with her son.

"She didn't even come into the house. We curled up on the spot where we met outside the house and went to sleep," said Deng, his eyes growing misty. "We stayed in that spot and cried tears of joy for four days."
Deng Kuol doesn't know if he'll ever see his mother or even his native country again. He wants to settle in Canada, and in fact right here in Kingston.
If he does return to Sudan, the 20-year-old bachelor will have some explaining to do.
"I'm supposed to have four wives by now," he said, flashing a grin.
